topic.name: Graphing Cubic Curves Containing a Double Root

question.text: Which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=(3-x)(1-x)^2?$
question.explanation:
The equation is already in factored form, so by the zero-product rule, we deduce that it has a single root at $x=3$ and a double root at $x=1.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation: \begin{align*} y &= (3-0)(1-0)^2 \\[3pt] &= (3)(1)^2 \\[3pt] &= 3. \end{align*}

So, the curve

  • intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,3),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=3,$ and

  • touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=1.$

Notice that the leading coefficient is negative:

\begin{align*} f(x) &= (3-x)(1-x)^2 \\[3pt] &= (3-x)(x^2-2x+1) \\[3pt] &= -x^3 + \cdots \end{align*}

question.text:
Given that $(x+5)$ is a factor of $f(x)=x^3+7x^2+11x+5$, which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+5)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+5)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+5)$ using synthetic division:

\[ \begin{array}{c|rrrr} & x^3 & x^2 &x^1 & x^0 \\ {\color{red}{-5}} & 1 & 7 & 11 & 5 \\ & & -5 & -10 & -5 \\ \hline & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \end{array} \]

Therefore,

\[ \dfrac{f(x)}{x+5} = x^2 + 2x + 1 \]

which means that

\[ f(x) = (x+5)(x^2 + 2x + 1). \]

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get \[ f(x) = (x+5)(x+1)^2. \]

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=-5$ and a double root at $x=-1.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

\begin{align*} y &= (0+5)(0+1)^2 \\ &= (5)(1)^2 \\ &= 5. \end{align*}

So, the curve

  • intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,5),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-5,$ and

  • touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-1.$

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

question.text:
Given that $x+3$ is a factor of $f(x)=-x^3 - 7 x^2 - 15 x - 9$, which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+3)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+3)$ using synthetic division:

\[ \begin{array}{c|rrrr} & x^3 & x^2 &x^1 & x^0 \\ {\color{red}{-3}} & -1 & -7 & -15 & -9 \\ & & 3 & 12 & 9 \\ \hline & -1 &-4 & -3 & 0 \end{array} \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \dfrac{f(x)}{x+3} &= -x^2 - 4x - 3 \\[5pt] &= -(x^2+4x+3) \end{align*}

which means that

\[ f(x) = -(x+3)(x^2+4x+3). \]

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get \[ f(x) = -(x+3)(x+1)(x+3)=-(x+1)(x+3)^2 \]

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=-1$ and a double root at $x=-3.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation: \begin{align*} y &= -(0+1)(0+3)^2 \\[3pt] &= -(1)(3)^2 \\[3pt] &= -9. \end{align*}

So, the curve

  • intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,-9),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-1,$ and

  • touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-3.$
